content.passage: When my family moved from Alexandria to a new city in the middle of the first term of the school year, I remember standing at the gate of my new school feeling like a stranger in my own country. Everyone already had their groups, their inside jokes, and their fixed seats in the cafeteria. For the first two weeks, I ate lunch alone, reading the same page of a book repeatedly without understanding a word of it. I told myself it did not matter. I was used to being independent, but by the end of each day, I felt strangely tired, as if pretending not to mind had used up more energy than the schoolwork itself. Belonging, I learned, is not something that is given to you on the first day. It is built slowly, through small and often unplanned moments. Mine began in the school garden, where a classmate noticed I was trying, badly, to identify a plant for a biology assignment. She corrected me, laughed, and then sat down to help, asking questions about my old school almost as an afterthought, as though getting to know me were the easiest thing in the world. That single conversation did not solve everything, but it cracked open a door. Psychologists describe belonging as a basic human need, not a luxury, positioned close to safety and listed among the things a person cannot easily do without. When students feel they belong, they take more risks in class and are less likely to withdraw when things go wrong. The opposite is also true: a student who feels unseen often stops raising their hand long before they stop caring about the subject. By the end of that first term, I had joined the school’s environmental club, mostly because of that one conversation in the garden, and I started arriving early to help set up the planting trays before class. I was no longer the new student who ate alone; I was someone with a seat, a role, and people who would notice if I were absent. What I now understand is that belonging is rarely about fitting into a group perfectly. It is about finding even one connection that quietly says, 'You are seen here.'
